title: Ezekiel 48:30–35
context: The Lord GOD describes the exits of the city: three gates on each side, named after the tribes of Israel, including Levi and a single gate for Joseph, with each side four thousand five hundred reeds. The city’s circumference is given, and the book closes with its new name: “The LORD is there.” The name answers the departure of the LORD’s glory from the temple (10:18–19; 11:23) and its return (43:1–5), and Revelation 21 also speaks of a city with gates named for the tribes and of God dwelling with his people (Rev 21:3, 12–13), which readers in both traditions name without harmonizing; both read the closing name as shared confession of God’s presence with his people.

verses.text: “These are the exits of the city: On the north side four thousand five hundred reeds by measure;
verses.arminianNotes:
“These are the exits of the city: On the north side four thousand five hundred reeds by measure.” Arminian readers note that the city’s gates are now described.

The square of 48:16 is recalled.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the city’s openness to the tribes.

Shared ground: both traditions read the gates as access for the whole people, and both hold the vision under several readings of chapters 40–48.

verses.text: and the gates of the city shall be named after the tribes of Israel, three gates northward: the gate of Reuben, one; the gate of Judah, one; the gate of Levi, one.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says “the gates of the city shall be named after the tribes of Israel”: on the north “the gate of Reuben …the gate of Judah …the gate of Levi.” Arminian readers note that Levi has a gate though not a land portion.

The whole people has a place in the city.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see all twelve tribes represented.

Shared ground: both traditions note the similar picture in Revelation 21:12, named without harmonizing.

verses.text: “At the east side four thousand five hundred reeds, and three gates: even the gate of Joseph, one; the gate of Benjamin, one; the gate of Dan, one.
verses.arminianNotes:
On the east side are three gates: “the gate of Joseph, one; the gate of Benjamin, one; the gate of Dan, one.” Arminian readers note that Joseph has one gate here, though two portions in the land.

With Levi included, the gates still number twelve.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the twelve tribes kept together in the city’s gates.

Shared ground: both traditions read the gate names as a picture of the whole people gathered around the city where the LORD dwells.

verses.text: “At the south side four thousand five hundred reeds by measure, and three gates: the gate of Simeon, one; the gate of Issachar, one; the gate of Zebulun, one.
verses.arminianNotes:
On the south side are “the gate of Simeon, one; the gate of Issachar, one; the gate of Zebulun, one.” Arminian readers note that the pattern continues.

Each side has three gates.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the order and symmetry of the city.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse simply as part of the gate list, without pressing meaning from the arrangement.

verses.text: “At the west side four thousand five hundred reeds, with their three gates: the gate of Gad, one; the gate of Asher, one; the gate of Naphtali, one.
verses.arminianNotes:
On the west side are “the gate of Gad, one; the gate of Asher, one; the gate of Naphtali, one.” Arminian readers note that the twelve gates are now complete.

The city is open on every side.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the completed design.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the twelve gates picture a reunited people, and both name Revelation 21:13 in passing.

verses.text: “It shall be eighteen thousand reeds in circumference; and the name of the city from that day shall be, ‘The LORD is there.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The city’s new name is given: “The LORD is there.” Arminian readers hear the book’s closing hope: the glory that departed (10:18–19) has returned (43:1–5).

God’s presence defines the city.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear the confession that God dwells with his people (cf. Rev 21:3).

Shared ground: both traditions read the name as a shared confession rather than a point of difference, whatever view they take of chapters 40–48, and rejoice that the LORD’s presence is the city’s identity.
